Louisiana Regulators Delay DraftKings' License Renewal Pending AI Investigation

Published October 18, 2026 · 4 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

The Louisiana Gaming Control Board voted unanimously on Thursday, October 15, to conditionally extend DraftKings' sports betting license rather than fully renew it, giving state investigators more time to look into allegations that the company used artificial intelligence to target its most vulnerable, losing bettors. DraftKings' license had been set to expire November 10.

A four-month bridge, not a renewal

Rather than approving a standard renewal at the hearing, held inside a House committee room at the state Capitol in Baton Rouge, the board granted a conditional extension running through February 19, 2027, with a full renewal hearing now scheduled for February 18. Board chair Hebert told DraftKings representatives that the move "is not a determination that DraftKings has engaged in any wrongdoing," but rather, in his words, "a measured regulatory response that allows us as a Board to fulfill our oversight responsibility."

The extension comes with seven specific conditions, including a requirement that DraftKings submit formal responses within 30 days about its use of artificial intelligence, its prediction-market activity, and its digital offerings to Louisiana residents, plus monthly compliance reports on the 15th of every month covering everything from responsible-gambling system changes to pending litigation.

What triggered the scrutiny

Much of the hearing centered on recent reporting alleging DraftKings uses AI models to identify and target bettors who are losing money, rather than simply tracking betting activity for ordinary business purposes. Assistant Attorney General Delancey Houston told the board the Louisiana State Police Gaming Enforcement Division "has concerns regarding recent allegations brought against DraftKings, and, therefore, additional time is needed to fully investigate those allegations." Separately, state investigators flagged that at least one DraftKings shareholder holding a 5% or greater stake had not yet completed the suitability vetting required of significant owners.

DraftKings co-founder Paul Liberman defended the company's practices at the hearing, saying, "We do not use AI in any way to target losing gamblers by any means," and noting the company tracks customer performance mainly for standard financial-reporting purposes rather than targeted marketing. He also pointed to DraftKings' 2025 move to eliminate credit-card deposits as evidence of its responsible-gambling posture, though Legal Sports Report's reporting noted other operators had already banned credit-card funding earlier.

Why it matters to bettors

DraftKings remains fully operational in Louisiana for now, and the conditional extension keeps the sportsbook running without interruption through at least mid-February. But the case adds Louisiana to a growing list of states scrutinizing how operators use customer data, following similar AI-targeting questions raised by regulators in Massachusetts and reported in national coverage. For bettors, the practical takeaway is that the underlying allegations remain unresolved and under active state investigation rather than decided either way — the board was explicit that a conditional renewal is not a finding against the company.
